sections.heading: 0 Course Structure and Time Allocation
points: Indicative timeline: Part I (12 h), Part II.1 (12 h), Part II.2 (6 h), Part III (6 h).
Exam 1 (February 9, 2026): MCQ (8 questions), 30 minutes, scope: Exercises 1–17, platform Evalmee.
Exam 2 (March 9, 2026): Written exam, 60 minutes, scope: all non-starred exercises, format paper.
Exam 3 (June 2026): Written exam, 90 minutes, scope: all non-starred exercises, format paper.
Exercises with (⋆) and Section 4 are for the Advanced Mathematics track and excluded from examinations.

sections.heading: 1 Determinant
points: Permutation / Symmetric group: Sn is the set of all bijections from [[1, n]] onto itself; Card(Sn) = n!.
Cycle and transposition: a p-cycle satisfies σ(x_k) = x_{k+1}, σ(x_p) = x_1, and fixes other elements; a 2-cycle is a transposition; Sn is generated by transpositions.
Signature: ε(σ) = (-1)^p where p is the count of transpositions in a decomposition; ε(σσ') = ε(σ)ε(σ').
Leibniz determinant formula: det(A) = sum_{σ ∈ Sn} ε(σ) prod_{i=1}^n A_{i,σ(i)}.
Geometric connection: columns of A form a basis of R^3 iff det(A) != 0; absolute determinant yields the volume of the parallelepiped generated by column vectors.
Linear system uniqueness and invertibility: ker(A) = {0} and unique solutions exist iff det(A) != 0.

Fibonacci and determinants: A = [[1, 1], [1, 0]] satisfies A^n = [[F_{n+1}, F_n], [F_n, F_{n-1}]]; det(A^n) yields Cassini's identity F_{n+1}F_{n-1} - F_n^2 = (-1)^n; diagonalization of A via eigenvalues phi and phi_bar yields Binet's formula F_n = (phi^n - phi_bar^n)/sqrt(5).

sections.heading: 2 Exercises on Endomorphism Reduction
points: Diagonalization condition: M = PDP^-1 with D diagonal and P in GL_n(R).
Spectrum and powers: if A is diagonalizable, A^2 is diagonalizable; converse does not generally hold; sums and products of diagonalizable matrices are not necessarily diagonalizable.
Rank and annihilating polynomials: A can be diagonalized via characteristic polynomial, rank considerations, or finding annihilating polynomials.
Cayley-Hamilton theorem: characteristic polynomial χ_C(X) annihilates matrix C (χ_C(C) = 0), useful for inverting matrices and deriving matrix powers C^n.
Applications to dynamical systems: predator-prey recurrence U_{n+1} = A U_n solved by computing A^n = P D^n P^-1.
Matrix exponential: exp(M) = I_n + sum_{k=1}^infinity M^k / k!; for diagonalizable M, exp(M) = P exp(D) P^-1, exp(0) = I_n, and det(exp(M)) = exp(Tr(M)).
Stochastic matrices: entries M_ij in [0, 1] with row sums equal to 1; always satisfy 1 in Sp(M), all eigenvalues |λ| <= 1, and M^n is stochastic for all n in N.

sections.heading: 3 Theoretical Exercises
points: Diagonalization theorem equivalences for A in M_n(R): (i) A is diagonalizable over R; (ii) χ_A(X) splits over R and algebraic multiplicity m_λ equals geometric multiplicity dim(E_λ) for all λ; (iii) dim(R^n) = sum dim(E_λ); (iv) R^n = direct sum of E_λ.
Determinant and trace of diagonalizable matrices: det(M) = prod_{i=1}^n λ_i and Tr(M) = sum_{i=1}^n λ_i.
Spectral invertibility criterion: 0 in Sp(M) <=> M is not invertible.
Matrix similarity (A ~ B <=> exists P in GL_n(R), A = PBP^-1): equivalence relation preserving determinant, trace, rank, characteristic polynomial, and spectrum (with multiplicities).
Multiplicity bound: for every λ in Sp(A), 1 <= dim(E_λ) <= m_λ.
Projection matrices: P^2 = P projects R^n onto Im(P) along ker(P); diagonalizable with Sp(P) subset of {0, 1}; R^n = ker(P) direct sum Im(P).
Nilpotent matrices (N^p = 0): Sp(N) = {0}, det(N) = 0, Tr(N) = 0; index of nilpotency <= n; symmetric nilpotent matrix is 0; for 2x2 matrices, nilpotent <=> det(A) = Tr(A) = 0.

sections.heading: 4 Optional Exercises
points: Vandermonde matrix: V(α_1, ..., α_n) with entries α_j^{i-1}; det(V_n) = V_{n-1} prod_{i=1}^{n-1} (α_n - α_i).
Limits of matrix powers: if lim_{n->infinity} A^n = B, then B is diagonalizable and Sp(B) subset of {0, 1}.

PageRank / Markov transitions: state distribution evolution X_{p+1} = X_p M => X_p = X_0 M^p; stationary vector v satisfies vM = v (eigenvector of M^T for λ = 1); damping factor matrix P = α M + (1 - α)(1/n)J.

Minimal polynomial µ_A: monic annihilating polynomial of lowest degree; µ_A divides every annihilating polynomial P and χ_A; Rac(µ_A) = Sp(A); A is diagonalizable iff µ_A splits into distinct linear factors.

key_terms.definition: The set of all bijections (permutations) from [[1, n]] onto itself, having cardinality n!.
A permutation σ in S_n cyclically mapping x_1 to x_2, ..., x_p to x_1, and leaving all other elements fixed.
The value ε(σ) = (-1)^p, where p is the number of transpositions in any decomposition of σ into transpositions.
The map defined by exp(M) = I_n + sum_{k=1}^infinity M^k / k!.
A square matrix M in M_n([0, 1]) such that the sum of the entries in each row equals 1: sum_{j=1}^n M_{ij} = 1 for all i.
Two matrices A, B in M_n(R) such that there exists an invertible matrix P in GL_n(R) with A = PBP^-1.
A matrix P in M_n(R) satisfying P^2 = P, projecting R^n onto Im(P) along ker(P).
A matrix M in M_n(R) such that M^p = 0 for some integer p >= 1; the smallest such p is the index of nilpotency.
A square matrix whose columns are successive powers of elements (α_1, ..., α_n), with entries V_{i,j} = α_j^{i-1}.
A probability vector v satisfying vM = v and sum_{i=1}^n v_i = 1 for a stochastic matrix M.
The unique monic polynomial µ_A of smallest degree that annihilates A (i.e., µ_A(A) = 0).
